lesson_title: Four Sentences That Save Your Project
hook_text: Two learners built rescue devices. One got full marks, one got nothing. The difference was written before they started.
clip_script: Two learners, same cardboard, same syringes. The first wrote a design brief: emergency workers need a tool to open crushed doors; I will make a working model of a hydraulic rescue device; syringes will drive lever jaws to show a big controlled force; built from the materials given in two weeks. Then two lists. Specifications, things you can test: jaws open 40 millimetres, hold a 50 gram block, stand alone. Constraints, the limits: only these materials, fits on A4, no sharp metal. Then three sketches, a table of ticks and crosses, a winner with reasons. The second learner wrote: I will make a rescue machine out of cardboard. Then built something. At the end, the teacher could test every promise the first learner made. The second had promised nothing, so nothing could be judged. The brief is your ruler. Write it first.
visual_style: Whiteboard split screen: left side a paragraph, two lists and a tick table; right side a single vague sentence and a question mark over a model.
mood: A fair warning with a clear fix.
pacing: Setup in one line, brisk tour of the brief and lists, slow landing on the comparison.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and write your own four-sentence brief tonight.
